extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, platform policymakers, researchers and students interested in misinformation and fake news
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for identifying, tracking, debunking, and platform-policymaking around fake news and fraudulent news websites, plus recommended consumer and technology responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check source, author, date, and headline
rubrics_metrics.description: FactCheck.org advised readers to check the source, author, date, and headline of publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FactCheck.org recommends verifying these basic metadata items and consulting other debunkers (Snopes, The Washington Post Fact Checker, PolitiFact.com). It also admonishes consumers to be wary of confirmation bias when evaluating stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tags/labels for debunked stories
rubrics_metrics.description: PolitiFact.com used a 'Fake news' tag so readers could view all stories Politifact had debunked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tagging debunked items lets readers aggregate and review previously labeled falsehoods; platforms can apply visible tags such as Facebook's 'disputed by third party fact-checkers' to flagged articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained debunking to be effective
rubrics_metrics.description: Full Fact argued that debunking must take place over a sustained period to be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-off corrections are unlikely to counteract repeated misinformation; sustained, continued fact-checking and outreach increases impact. Full Fact also worked with Google on automation to assist sustained efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deny advertising revenue to deceptive sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Google and Facebook moved to ban ads from sites with deceptive content and deny ad revenue to fraudulent news providers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Banning monetization (e.g., via AdSense) reduces the financial incentive for creating fake sites. Google stated the ban targets companies that lie about their purpose, content, or publisher; satire may be an exception though some satirical sites risk being inadvertently blocked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demote and warn (rather than fully remove) disputed content
rubrics_metrics.description: Facebook applied warning labels such as 'disputed by third party fact-checkers' and intended disputed articles to show up farther down in the News Feed while still allowing sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample warning tested: 'This website is not a reliable news source. Reason: Classification Pending'. Facebook's rollout was initially limited and in testing; TechCrunch noted potential for false positives. Users can still share tagged articles but they are de-emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partner with third-party fact-checkers (IFCN code)
rubrics_metrics.description: Facebook formed partnerships with fact-checking groups that had joined the Poynter International Fact-Checking Network (IFCN) fact-checkers' code of principles to help debunk fraud on the site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-party fact-checkers (e.g., ABC News, The Washington Post, Snopes, FactCheck.org, PolitiFact, AP) verify content and trigger platform labels; Facebook did not finance the fact-checkers and expected increased traffic to their sites as a result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide user reporting options for false stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Facebook users were given the option to report posts with 'I think it shouldn't be on Facebook' followed by 'It's a false news story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowd-sourced reporting allows users to flag suspicious posts for review; this was among measures Facebook considered and implemented to surface questionable material for further checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect website spoofing and domain impersonation
rubrics_metrics.description: Facebook planned to employ staff researchers to determine whether website spoofing had occurred (for example 'washingtonpost.co' vs the real 'washingtonpost.com').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform-level domain checks and researcher review can identify impersonation tactics used by fake news purveyors and help prevent misattribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic demotion and search-ranking changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Google announced changes to search algorithms to stop the 'spread of blatantly misleading, low quality, offensive or downright false information' and later banned deceptive sites from profiting via AdSense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search and feed ranking adjustments can reduce the visibility of low-quality and deceptive content; algorithmic changes may have uneven effects and have been criticized as potentially removing legitimate anti-establishment sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and deploy user-facing tools to warn about fraudulent sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed technology tools included a Google Chrome extension to warn users about fraudulent news sites and open-source initiatives to develop design solutions for fake news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools can be browser-based warnings, community-curated databases, or open-source models. Proposals included a ratings organization analogous to the Better Business Bureau and a Wikipedia-like database of media producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate consumers to behave like fact-checkers (scientific method approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers recommended educating online media consumers to themselves behave like fact-checkers and applying the scientific method to fake news analysis: Observe, Question, Hypothesize, Analyze data, Draw conclusion, Act on results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific suggested checks: check the URL, article date, evaluate reader/writer bias, double-check the evidence, and verify cited sources. Stanford study found many students could not distinguish sponsored content from news, supporting education-focused interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider and test moderation measures carefully (balance and unintended effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms considered but did not implement measures such as user-tagging of questionable material, fully automated checking tools, and third-party confirmation; some responses (algorithm changes, ad bans) drew criticism for potential overreach or inadvertent blocking of legitimate sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy changes should be piloted and their impacts monitored (e.g., the World Socialist Web Site reported drops in referrals after Google's April 25 algorithm changes and characterized the moves as suppressing anti-establishment voices). Transparency and safeguards against false positives are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification categories and curator transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic and grassroots lists (e.g., Melissa Zimdars' 'False, Misleading, Clickbait-y, and/or Satirical' handout) and aggregator tools (Junk News Aggregator) classify sources and track engagement from junk news sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curated lists and aggregators help researchers and the public identify recurring fraudulent outlets and measure spread; maintainers should clarify purpose (teaching vs public blacklist) to avoid misinterpretation and update categories over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use data-driven monitoring to target interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Research findings suggested fake news sharing is concentrated (a small percentage of users account for most sharing) and that demographic factors (e.g., age) influence sharing behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms and policymakers can use empirical findings (who shares, concentration of spreaders, topical patterns) to design targeted interventions (e.g., focus on high-impact accounts or demographic-tailored education).
